corrected_value.authors: Drake, C. E., Primeaux, S., & Thomas, J.
corrected_value.title: Comparing implicit gender stereotypes between women and men with the Implicit Relational Assessment Procedure.

decision.quote: The present study systematically replicated the procedures of Drake et al. (2018) and employed the IRAP to assess general gender stereotypes among Japanese university students, who live in a society where gender inequality remains a pressing issue. In the IRAP procedure, participants responded to pairings of binary gender labels (female and male) and trait descriptors (feminine and masculine) by selecting “true” or “false” under instructions emphasizing rapid responding. Participants exhibited response patterns that were primarily pro-congruent with gender stereotypes, reflected in a consistent tendency to affirm matched gender label–trait pairings (i.e., female–feminine and male–masculine). No significant gender differences were found. Nevertheless, we discussed the possibility of stronger stereotype-consistent responses among male participants in pairings involving male labels, as implied by the current data. Correlational analyses were also conducted between the IRAP performances and scores on an explicit measure of egalitarian attitudes, although no clear correlations were found in the majority of analyses. Overall, the results generally replicated those of Drake et al. (2018), demonstrating stereotype-consistent responses in a Japanese sample.
decision.reason: The title and abstract explicitly state that the study is a systematic replication of Drake et al. (2018), re-testing implicit general gender stereotypes (binary gender label and feminine/masculine trait pairings on the IRAP, gender differences, and correlations with explicit egalitarian attitudes) in a new sample of Japanese university students and comparing the empirical findings directly against Drake et al. (2018). The reference list verifies the full bibliographic identity of Drake, Primeaux, & Thomas (2018) in Gender Issues, 35, 3–20, DOI 10.1007/s12147-017-9189-6. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 443) is Scanlon et al. (2014) (DOI 10.1037/h0100577), a completely different paper examining implicit gender bias and self-esteem in children with ADHD and dyslexia; report equivalence does not apply. No prior adjudication file existed for this work.

decision.quote: In their paper of 2011 titled Gender and Philosophical Intuition Wesley Buckwalter and Stephen Stich argue that the intuitions of women and men differ significantly on various types of philosophical questions. Furthermore, men’s intuitions, so the authors, are more in line with traditionally accepted solutions of classical problems. This inherent bias, so the argument, is one of the factors that leads more men than women to pursue degrees and careers in philosophy. We attempted to replicate three of the classes of questions that Buckwalter and Stich review in their paper and for which they report significant differences. We failed to replicate the results. In specific we attempted replication of Section 3.2 and 3.8 in Buckwalter and Stich (2011).
decision.reason: The abstract explicitly states that the author empirically re-tested the gender differences in philosophical intuitions reported in Sections 3.1, 3.2, and 3.8 of Wesley Buckwalter and Stephen Stich (2011), titled 'Gender and Philosophical Intuition', in new participant samples and failed to find significant gender differences. Although only the title and abstract are available in the primary source text, the abstract itself explicitly provides the target's authors, year (2011), exact title, and empirical comparison; no DOI is printed in the source text. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 521) is Knobe (2012) ('Experimental Philosophy', DOI 10.1093/oxfordhb/9780195309799.013.0022), a different author's handbook chapter that is not an alternate report of Buckwalter and Stich (2011). No prior adjudication file existed for this work.
